strengths: The paper provides a clean, principled formulation of neuron-level fusion as a representation-matching problem, with a interpretable decomposition into grouping and approximation errors (Theorem 1) and concrete algorithmic instantiations (Hungarian Fusion, K-means Fusion, linear and gradient variants).

It offers theoretical grounding: optimality of Hungarian Fusion in the pairwise equal-size case and a (9+ε)-approximation guarantee for K-means Fusion via known local-search results, with proofs provided in the appendix.

The integration of neuron attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into fusion is a genuinely novel angle, and the authors also show these scores improve existing baselines (Git Re-Basin, OTFusion), which strengthens the generality of the claim (Tables 11, 15).

Experiments cover three data regimes (non-IID, sharded, full-dataset), two architectures (VGG11, ViT), multiple seeds, runtime comparisons (Tables 6-7), and qualitative analyses (importance-score histograms, clustering visualization, loss landscapes). The gains in zero-shot non-IID/sharded fusion, where OTFusion and Git Re-Basin fail badly, are convincing (Tables 1, 2, 8, 9).
Reproducibility is well handled: detailed hyperparameters for training and fusion, data partitioning procedures, licensing of reused assets, and an open-source code repository.
The limitations section is honest and specific (hyperparameter sensitivity of the gradient variant, data-size dependency, lack of universality claims).
weaknesses: Scale and breadth of evaluation are limited: only VGG11 on CIFAR-10 and a small custom ViT on CIFAR-100. Claims of generality to 'any differentiable DNN architecture' are not tested beyond these two settings; no larger models, ImageNet-scale data, or language models.

Several comparisons are missing or restricted: Transformer OTFusion (Imfeld et al.) was not benchmarked despite being the most relevant prior work for ViTs; full knowledge distillation was dismissed due to overfitting and replaced with a last-layer KD variant, which weakens the baseline comparison in non-IID setups.

The experimental protocol reports the best result across importance-score choices per seed ('we report the result with the best-performing importance score'), which is a form of oracle selection that can bias headline numbers in the paper's favor; full tables mitigate but do not eliminate this concern.

The hyperparameter settings for the gradient variant differ per experiment (Setting 1 vs. Setting 2 assigned by setup, e.g., 'All Non-IID models, except... used Setting 2'), and Appendix F admits Setting 2 gains come mainly from fitting averaged logits at the classification head - close to a KD-like procedure - raising questions about how much of the improvement stems from the proposed representation-matching objective versus distillation-style fitting.

The theoretical contributions are somewhat incremental: Theorem 1 is a standard weighted K-means-style decomposition, and Theorem 2(b) largely transfers the known (9+ε) bound of Kanungo et al. to this setting.

Presentation issues: the abstract's code URL is empty; Table 3 is garbled with merged rows and misaligned columns, making the full-dataset ViT results hard to read; there are minor grammatical errors throughout.

The method requires fusion data, and the amount used varies substantially across experiments (400 samples for VGG, 6000-7000 for ViT), complicating fair assessment of data efficiency versus KD baselines.

strengths: The paper presents a clean conceptual framing of model fusion as a representation-matching problem, decomposed into an interpretable grouping error and approximation error (Theorem 1), which motivates a concrete two-stage algorithm (Hungarian Fusion / K-means Fusion).

The experimental coverage is broad relative to typical fusion papers: non-IID (Dirichlet), sharded, and full-dataset regimes, with multiple seeds (5 for non-IID), multiple architectures (VGG11, small ViT), and supplementary tables reporting results per importance score (Tables 11-15), which improves transparency.

The paper demonstrates that retro-fitting neuron importance scores into Git Re-Basin (Table 11: 53.8 → 71.8 on 2-way non-IID) improves a strong baseline, which is a useful, transferable insight independent of the proposed method.

Limitations are discussed honestly (hyperparameter sensitivity of the gradient variant, data-size dependence, slowdowns in Table 7), and reproducibility is supported by code, detailed hyperparameter tables (Table 5), and a runtime comparison.

The zero-shot non-IID results (e.g., 69.6% at 8-way split where OTFusion gets 12.9% and last-layer KD 43.7%) are striking and, if robust, represent a meaningful practical gain for federated-style fusion.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty is overstated. The abstract claims the algorithms are 'the first to successfully incorporate neuron importance scores in model fusion', yet Appendix C concedes OTFusion (Singh and Jaggi, 2020) already used neuron importance as the probability measure in the OT problem. The core contribution is essentially OTFusion/Git Re-Basin-style neuron matching combined with (a) refitting fused weights to match cluster targets and (b) weighted K-means — incremental refinements over known techniques rather than a new family.

There is a double standard in the 'zero-shot' framing. Permutation-based baselines align and average weights without gradient training, whereas the proposed method fits each level's weights with 50-100 epochs of Adam/SGD per level on fusion data (up to 7000 samples; 632s for one ViT fusion per Table 7). Calling the baselines 'non-zero-shot' for requiring fine-tuning while the proposed method trains every level on held data obscures this distinction; a fair comparison would give baselines the same data/gradient budget.

The gains of the gradient variant appear substantially confounded by a head-fitting/distillation effect. The authors themselves admit (Appendix F.1) that under Setting 2 'the majority of performance gain occurs at the classification head... This is similar to Knowledge Distillation', and the 'Head Weights' heuristic reweights logits by class proportions. This undermines the claim that performance comes from neuron-level interpolation, and no ablation isolates the head-fitting contribution.

Cherry-picking is a concern: 'Each fusion algorithm is applied once per neuron importance score, and we report the result with the best-performing importance score' (Section 5.2). Combined with per-setup switching between hyperparameter Settings 1 and 2 (Appendix F.1), the reported numbers may not generalize, and the hyperparameter search protocol is not fully described.

The baseline comparison is incomplete and selectively favorable. Transformer OTFusion (Imfeld et al., 2023) and FedMA are not run (timeline excuse); Git Re-Basin and HF are marked N/A for >2-way splits in Tables 1 and 9 rather than being extended (Git Re-Basin supports multi-model fusion in principle); and KD is restricted to last-layer with an ad hoc justification, while full KD is a natural and strong baseline.

The evaluation scale is small and misaligned with the motivation. The introduction motivates fusion by the cost of 'large' models and data scarcity, yet all experiments use VGG11 and a 7-block/384-hidden ViT on CIFAR-10/100. No evidence is given that the method scales — indeed the linear KF variant is ~100x slower than OTFusion (78.3s vs 0.7s), and the runtime grows steeply with fusion samples (38s at 400 → 632s at 6000).

The theoretical results are thin. Theorem 1 is a standard K-means bias-variance decomposition, and Theorem 2 largely imports known results (Hungarian optimality for LSAP; the (9+ε) bound of Kanungo et al.) to the fusion setting; neither addresses the actually hard question of how per-level errors compound across levels, which is the paper's own stated hypothesis (Section 3).

In the full-dataset setting, the headline claim 'consistently outperform previous fusion techniques' weakens: zero-shot fused ViTs score 72.7 vs base models at 73.4 (Table 3/14), only surpassing baselines after fine-tuning, and Table 10 shows fused VGGs roughly match (91.0 vs 91.2) rather than beat base models zero-shot.

Presentation issues reduce polish: the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('The code is available at:' with no URL), there are repeated typos ('does allows', 'when when', 'In practice we as we'), and Algorithm 1/notation occasionally obscure what is actually computed (e.g., clustering over activation vectors vs. neuron parameters).

strengths: Clear and principled formulation: the paper decomposes fusion into a neuron-aware representation cost that splits into an interpretable grouping error and approximation error (Theorem 1), yielding a natural two-stage algorithm (Hungarian Fusion and K-means Fusion variants).

Non-trivial theoretical support: Theorem 2(a) gives optimality of Hungarian Fusion for equal-size linear levels, and Theorem 2(b) gives a (9+epsilon)-approximation guarantee for K-means Fusion via the Kanungo et al. local-search algorithm, with a proof that carefully handles the projection of activations onto the reachable subspace.

Genuine algorithmic novelty: incorporating neuron attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into both clustering (weighted K-means) and target computation is a new angle, and the ablations (Table 11, Table 13) plus the retrofitting of scores into Git Re-Basin show the improvement is not merely architectural.

Strong empirical results in the hard regimes: in non-IID and sharded setups the proposed methods substantially outperform OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, vanilla averaging, and last-layer KD (e.g., 84.6 vs 71.8 on 2-way non-IID CIFAR-10; 69.6 vs 12.9 OTFusion on 8-way), approaching ensemble performance at a fraction of inference cost.

Comprehensive experimental hygiene: multiple seeds, three data regimes, runtime comparisons (Tables 6-7), per-importance-score breakdowns in the appendix, detailed hyperparameter documentation, and an honest limitations section discussing hyperparameter sensitivity and data-size dependence.

Generality claim is supported in principle: the level-based formulation accommodates convolutions and transformer blocks, demonstrated on both VGG11 and ViT, and handles arbitrary model widths via clustering rather than one-to-one matching.
weaknesses: Overstated novelty claim: the paper claims to be 'the first to successfully incorporate neuron importance scores in model fusion', yet Appendix C itself notes that OTFusion (Singh and Jaggi, 2020) already used neuron importance as the probability measure in the OT formulation. The contribution should be framed more carefully.
Incomplete abstract: 'The code is available at:' ends without a URL. For a paper whose reproducibility argument rests on an open-source repository, this is a material omission that must be fixed.

Limited empirical scope: all experiments use CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 with VGG11 and a small ViT. The claim of working on 'any differentiable DNN architecture' is demonstrated on only two architectures at modest scale; no ImageNet, no language models, and no comparison to the Transformer OTFusion baseline on shared footing (relied instead on reported numbers with much weaker base models).

Potential selection bias in reporting: main tables report the best-performing importance score per setting; while the appendix discloses all scores, the headline numbers are test-set-selected among multiple variants, which slightly inflates apparent gains.

Theory-practice gap: the guarantees (Theorem 2) apply only to affine levels, whereas the best-performing variant in the harder regimes (KF Gradient, used for ViTs and sharded setups) is a heuristic SGD procedure with no theoretical backing, is hyperparameter-sensitive (two ad hoc settings chosen per regime), and depends on fusion-set size (Table 7 shows ~16x runtime growth).

Data-access assumptions deserve more scrutiny: the zero-shot claim relies on using 400-7000 samples 'from the dataset seen by the first model', which weakens the data-privacy motivation given in the introduction and is not discussed in the limitations.

In full-dataset fine-tuning regime, gains over baselines are modest and the method sometimes trails fine-tuned base models (Table 3: 74.5 fused+FT vs base models at 74.2+), so the significance outside heterogeneous-data settings is less clear.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and well-motivated formulation of model fusion as an importance-weighted representation-matching problem, with a clean decomposition of the representation cost into grouping and approximation errors (Theorem 1) and useful approximation guarantees for Hungarian and K-means variants (Theorem 2), including a rigorous (9+eps)-approximation argument via the Kanungo et al. local-search result.

The evaluation is notably broad and thorough: three architectures (VGG, ResNet, ViT), three data regimes (sharded, non-IID, full dataset), multiple seeds, ablations over fusion-dataset size, importance scores, width mismatches, compression-as-fusion, a realistic medical scenario (BloodMNIST), and a comparison against ZipIt! on ImageNet-1k.

The zero-shot non-IID/sharded setting is a genuinely difficult regime where prior methods (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, Transformer OTFusion) collapse to near-random performance, and the proposed methods demonstrably remain functional there—this is a real, previously unmet capability.

Limitations are discussed honestly and in detail (hyperparameter sensitivity of gradient variants, dependence on fusion-dataset size, slower runtimes), with runtime tables (Tables 10-12) that contextualize overhead relative to fine-tuning costs rather than hiding it.

The attribution-score integration is evaluated carefully, including an analysis of how importance scores shift clustering behavior (Figure 3), and is shown to help both their methods and baselines like Git Re-Basin.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core recipe—align neurons level-by-level and refit the level's weights to matched targets—is closely related to PLeaS (Nasery et al., 2025, cited but not compared against), FedMA's layerwise alignment, and stage-wise knowledge distillation; the paper acknowledges the ResNet compression experiment 'can be interpreted as stage-wise knowledge distillation.' The main distinctions (importance weighting, refitting accumulated error, general DAG-of-levels support) are meaningful but modest.

The 'zero-shot' framing is somewhat overstated: the gradient-based variants require a fusion dataset (up to 25k samples on ImageNet-1k) and substantial optimization per level, which is effectively a constrained training procedure rather than training-free fusion. Performance also degrades noticeably with smaller fusion sets (Table 7, Table 4).

The theory is modest: Theorem 1 is a straightforward algebraic identity, and Theorem 2's approximation guarantee applies only to affine levels with previous levels fixed—a condition the algorithm only approximately satisfies in practice for nonlinear levels.

Baseline comparisons are not uniformly favorable: linear probing (LP) is competitive with or better than several proposed variants in some settings (e.g., Table 13: LP 85.5 vs. KF-Gradient ~84; Table 14 8-way: LP 73.8 vs. KF variants ~69), and KD sometimes wins (Table 2, 4-way/6-way: KD 47.0/43.6 vs. KF-Gradient 41.4/34.7). The headline claims of consistent superiority should be tempered.

Presentation issues reduce polish: garbled characters in Section F.5 ('âA˘TIt'), duplicated phrases ('keep the weights of keep the weights', 'as we as we primarily tested'), the code URL is missing from the abstract, and inconsistent details (200 vs. 100 fine-tuning epochs between Section F.3 and Table 12) raise reproducibility concerns despite extensive appendix documentation.
No experiments at larger scale (LLMs or even larger vision models), so generality claims about 'any DAG-modularizable architecture' remain empirically limited to small/medium vision models.

strengths: The paper identifies real and well-documented gaps in the model fusion literature (limited zero-shot/non-IID evaluation, per-architecture re-implementations, weak base models) and addresses them with a coherent neuron-centric framework that treats fusion as representation matching with importance-weighted centroids as targets.

The two-stage decomposition (grouping error vs. approximation error) is clean and interpretable; Theorem 1's decomposition and Theorem 2's level-wise guarantees (optimality for Hungarian Fusion, (9+eps)-approximation for K-means Fusion via Kanungo et al.) give the algorithm a principled foundation, and the proofs in Appendix A appear correct.

Experimental coverage is unusually broad: VGGs, ResNets, and ViTs across sharded, non-IID, and full-dataset regimes; a direct comparison with ZipIt! on ImageNet-1k; width-mismatch fusion; compression-as-fusion; runtime breakdowns; and honest reporting of full result tables with all importance-score variants.

The sharded/non-IID results are convincing: baseline fusion methods (OTFusion, Transformer OTFusion, vanilla averaging) collapse to near-random accuracy, while KF/HF variants retain meaningful zero-shot performance, and the BloodMNIST and ImageNet experiments suggest practical relevance for federated/one-shot settings.

The limitations section is candid (hyperparameter sensitivity of gradient variants, data-efficiency, slower runtime), and the runtime analysis (Tables 10-12) contextualizes overhead rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than strong. HF is close to activation-based Git Re-Basin/OTFusion plus level-wise refitting, and KF resembles FedMA-style layer-wise alignment; the connection to PLeaS-merging (Nasery et al., 2025), which also combines permutation with per-layer least squares, deserves a deeper discussion than it receives. The main deltas are the level-wise retrofitting and importance weighting.

There is some overclaiming relative to the evidence. The claim of 'consistent improvements over existing methods' is weakened by the paper's own tables: Linear Probing beats all KF variants on the 8-way non-IID CIFAR-10 split (73.8 vs 71.6), KD beats KF-Gradient on the 4-way sharded ViT CIFAR-100 split (47.0 vs 41.4), and fused models remain substantially below the ensemble in most zero-shot settings (e.g., 54.5 vs 63.7).

A methodological red flag: Table 3 reports, per algorithm, 'the result with the importance scores that result in the best accuracy,' which appears to be test-set selection. With three importance-score variants per algorithm, per-table best-score cherry-picking (as in Tables 3 and 4) can inflate headline numbers; the full appendix tables partially mitigate but do not eliminate this concern.

The importance-score contribution, advertised as a key innovation, is empirically weak: uniform scores are often within noise of Conductance/DeepLIFT (e.g., Table 15: HF-Gradient Uniform 88.1 vs DeepLIFT 88.1; Table 18/19 differences are ~0.5-1%), and Table 8 shows uniform sometimes best. The 'first to incorporate neuron importance scores' claim is thin given Singh & Jaggi (2020) already used importance as the OT probability measure, as the paper itself acknowledges in Appendix C.

Theoretical guarantees are level-wise and assume fixed preceding weights; no guarantee connects the greedy level-wise procedure to end-to-end fused-model quality, and the decomposition theorem is essentially an algebraic identity. The theory is supportive but not deep.

Gradient-based variants require substantial fusion data (up to 25k samples on ImageNet) and are sensitive to hyperparameters; the practical zero-shot advantage over LP, which is simpler and competitive in several regimes, is not clearly established. Several presentation defects remain (e.g., 'keep the weights of keep the weights of', encoding artifact 'âA˘T' in Section F.5, citation to 'NeurIPS 2026' as LMC evidence).

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies genuine gaps in model fusion research (zero-shot fusion under non-IID/sharded data, base-model quality, reproducibility) and the experiments directly target these gaps.

Principled formulation: the representation cost in Eq. (1) with its decomposition into grouping and approximation errors (Theorem 1) is clean, interpretable, and leads naturally to a two-stage algorithm; the proofs in Section A are correct and clearly written.

Theoretical results, while modest, are appropriate: optimality of Hungarian Fusion in the pairwise equal-size case and a (9+ε)-approximation guarantee for K-means Fusion via Kanungo et al. (2002), with honest discussion of the necessary fixed-previous-levels assumption.

Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: VGGs, ResNets, and ViTs across CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1k; multiple regimes (sharded, non-IID, full dataset); comparisons to OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, ZipIt!, KD, LP, and ensembles; plus a plausible real-world scenario (BloodMNIST) and a compression use case where the method substantially beats data-limited KD (70.6% vs 45.9%).

The neuron attribution (Conductance/DeepLIFT) integration is a genuinely novel ingredient, shown both to improve baselines (Git Re-Basin) and to materially alter clustering behavior (Figure 3, adjusted Rand indices).

Good transparency on limitations (hyperparameter sensitivity, data efficiency, runtime) with runtime breakdowns (Tables 10-12) that contextualize the overhead, and an open-source reimplementation supporting reproducibility.
Robustness studies (fusion dataset size, augmentation, varying widths) address natural objections, and the ImageNet-1k comparison with ZipIt! strengthens external validity.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: refitting weights to match activation targets is closely related to staged knowledge distillation to intermediate activations, and the authors themselves note KD and LP are special cases of their framework; the main new elements are the clustering-based grouping and importance weighting. The conceptual delta over OTFusion/Git Re-Basin (refit rather than permute-and-average) is real but incremental.

In the full-dataset setting, zero-shot fused models still substantially underperform individual base models and ensembles (e.g., 63.0% vs. 73.9% base on CIFAR-100 ViT), and fine-tuned gains over Transformer OTFusion are modest (+1.4%); the headline strength is concentrated in the sharded/non-IID zero-shot regime.

Potential test-set leakage in model/score selection: several tables (e.g., Table 3, Tables 13-22) report results 'with the importance scores that result in the best accuracy', suggesting that the attribution method was selected on test accuracy rather than via a validation protocol, which inflates the reported advantage over baselines.

HF variants are N/A for >2-way fusion, so the multi-model results rest entirely on KF; the family framing in Table 1 somewhat oversells coverage, and the self-assessment table is favorable by construction.

Gradient-based variants are hyperparameter-sensitive and data-hungry (acknowledged), and runtimes are 15-100x slower than lightweight baselines; the justification is reasonable but limits practicality.
Theoretical guarantees apply only to affine levels with frozen preceding levels; behavior for the practically important non-linear/gradient variants is unsupported by theory.

Presentation polish issues: typos ('keep the weights of keep the weights of previous levels frozen', 'we as we primarily tested'), encoding artifacts in Section F.5 ('â ĄT'), and an apparently mis-dated citation (Theus et al., 2026).

Generality claims ('any architecture modularizable as a DAG of levels') are validated on only three vision architecture families; no language-model or other-modality experiments, which is fine but weakens the scope claim.
